title: Weathering, Erosion and Deposition
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Weathering, Erosion and Deposition Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition cause slow or rapid change to Earth's surface (Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition, with Australian landforms such as the Twelve Apostles and Uluru. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Weathering breaks rock, erosion and transportation move it, deposition drops it.
body_html:
How to think about it

Four processes change the land: weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition.

  • Weathering breaks rock where it is (ice in cracks, roots, heat and cold, water dissolving limestone).
  • Erosion picks the pieces up; transportation carries them by water, wind, ice, waves or gravity.
  • Deposition drops them where the water or wind slows down: river mouths, beaches, behind fences.
Example

Ice splits a rock. Which process?

the rock breaks but does not move

Answer: weathering

Example

A river drops mud at its mouth. Which process?

the water slows down

it cannot carry the mud

Answer: deposition

Common mistakes

  • Calling the breaking of rock erosion (that is weathering).
  • Thinking deposition happens where water is fastest.
  • Thinking all changes to the land are slow (landslides and floods are fast).

faq.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
faq.a: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is. Erosion picks up and moves those pieces away.

faq.q: How did the Twelve Apostles form?
faq.a: Waves eroded caves in the limestone cliffs. The caves became arches, and when the arches collapsed, stacks of rock were left standing.
Plant grass and trees, build windbreaks and retaining walls, keep stock away from riverbanks and stay on paths in sand dunes.

items.q: Dust blown from the outback travels across the sea to New Zealand. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Which of these is caused by deposition?
c: a sandbar at the mouth of a creek
a cliff falling into the sea
items.e: A sandbar forms where sand is dropped.

items.q: Which force pulls rocks and soil downhill in a landslide?
items.e: Gravity pulls everything down.

items.q: A muddy river carries soil many kilometres downstream. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Cattle trample a riverbank and the soil is washed away. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: What can farmers plant to reduce wind erosion?
items.e: Windbreaks slow the wind.

items.q: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and makes a cave. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Why are rocks in a river usually smooth and round?
c: Water and other rocks wore down their sharp edges.
items.e: Weathering by moving water smooths rocks over time.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes third?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Uluru is made of sandstone. How did its surface get its caves and grooves?
c: Weathering and erosion over millions of years
items.e: These are very slow changes.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes first?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: What is erosion?
c: the breaking of rock into smaller pieces
the moving of rock pieces and soil to a new place
items.e: Water, wind, ice and gravity cause erosion.

items.q: What is deposition?
c: the dropping of moved rock and soil in a new place
items.e: Deltas and sand dunes form by deposition.

items.q: Pebbles roll and bounce along the bed of a fast river. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Why do pebbles in a river become round?
c: They knock against each other and wear away their sharp edges.
items.e: This happens as they are transported.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes last?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Which happens first?
c: They all happen at the same time always.
items.e: Rock must be broken before the pieces can be carried.

items.q: How does ice weather rock?
c: Water freezes in cracks, expands and pushes the rock apart.
items.e: Water gets bigger when it freezes.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes second?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Which change is usually slowest?
c: a storm washing away a beach
items.e: Weathering by wind can take thousands of years.

items.q: Mei reads: “A cave forms as water dissolves rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes thousands of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Noah reads: “Layers of mud pile up and turn into rock.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: millions of years.

items.q: Noah reads: “A big storm wave knocks down part of a sand dune.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hours, so it is fast.

items.q: Waves wear away the bottom of a cliff and carry the pieces off. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Sand blasts against a rock in a dust storm and smooths it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Salt crystals grow in tiny holes in a sea cliff and crumble the sandstone. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Which word means rock breaking into smaller pieces without being moved?
items.e: Weathering happens in place.

items.q: Loose soil slides down a hillside cut for a new road. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Where does a river drop most of its sand and mud?
c: at the fastest part of the river
where it slows down, such as at its mouth
at the top of a waterfall
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Floodwater digs out the bank of a creek on a bend. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Boulders tumble down a gorge wall and pile up at the bottom. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: On Kosciuszko, freezing nights crack rocks on the mountain top. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is ice.

items.q: Waves crash against the coast and wear away the cliffs. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: A storm surge washes away the front of a sand dune at the beach. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Layers of sand settle at the bottom of a lake over many years. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: A river slows down where it meets the sea and drops mud, forming new land. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: A tree root grows into a crack and slowly pushes the rock apart. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: A desert rock is shaped like a mushroom by sand blowing near the ground. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Ethan reads: “Tree roots crack a big rock.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: many years.

items.q: Fine sand is blown off a ploughed field on a windy day. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Sand settles on the inside bend of a river where the water is slow. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Ruby reads: “Wind and rain wear a big rock into sand.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes thousands of years, so it is slow.

items.q: After a flood, a layer of mud is left on the farm paddocks. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: A flood washes a gully into a paddock. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the gibber plains in the outback?
items.e: Wind blew away the fine sand and left the stones behind.

items.q: William reads: “A rock falls off a cliff.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes seconds, so it is fast.

items.q: Which word means dropping sand, mud or pebbles in a new place?
items.e: Deposition happens when the moving water or wind slows down.

items.q: Lichen growing on a rock slowly breaks down its surface. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Sand is pushed along a beach by waves arriving at an angle. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Why did the trays with plants lose less soil in Priya's test?
c: Plant roots hold the soil in place.
items.e: Roots act like a net that holds soil.

items.q: Aarav reads: “An earthquake shakes the ground and cracks a road.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: seconds or minutes.

items.q: A glacier carries boulders as it slowly moves down a valley. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Waves drop sand in a sheltered bay, making a wide beach. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Which process mainly formed Wave Rock in Western Australia?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Weathering under the soil and rain shaped the curved granite face.

items.q: Ocean swell slowly wears down a rock platform. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Pebbles on a beach are rolled smooth by the sea. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Which process mainly formed Kings Canyon in the Northern Territory?
items.e: Water and weathering cut deep into the sandstone.

items.q: Sand dunes slowly move inland across the coast. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Harper reads: “A river carves a deep canyon.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Matilda sprinkled the same amount of water on three trays of soil. Which tray lost the least soil?
c: They all lost the same amount.
items.e: The tray with small bushes lost only 40 g.

items.q: Mia sees a pile of sand where a stream enters a lake. What happened there?
items.e: The water slowed down and dropped the sand.

items.q: Hamish reads: “A flood fills a town's streets with water.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hours or days, so it is fast.

items.q: Heavy rain washes soil off a bare hillside. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Twelve Apostles in Victoria?
items.e: Waves eroded the limestone cliffs, leaving stacks of rock.

items.q: Priya reads: “Ocean waves wear away a rocky cliff.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: hundreds of years.

items.q: A town wants to stop a hill from eroding onto a road. Which solution would help most?
c: cut down the trees on the hill
plant grass and build a retaining wall
items.e: Plants and walls hold soil in place.

items.q: William reads: “Tree roots crack a big rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes many years, so it is slow.

items.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock, freezes, expands and splits the rock. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Chloe wants to test how wind erodes sand. Which tool helps her make wind?
items.e: She can change the fan speed and measure how far the sand moves.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the wide floodplain beside the Hawkesbury River?
items.e: Floods dropped layers of mud on the land.

items.q: Strong wind picks up loose sand from a dune. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Jenolan Caves in New South Wales?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Water slowly dissolved the limestone.

items.q: Why do farmers plant rows of trees along the edges of fields?
c: to block wind and reduce wind erosion
items.e: Windbreaks slow the wind.

items.q: A fast creek scrapes sand and pebbles from its banks. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Which measurement shows how fast a beach is eroding?
c: the width of the beach each year
items.e: If the beach gets narrower each year, sand is being eroded.

items.q: Aarav puts chalk pieces in a jar of water and shakes it for 5 minutes. The chalk becomes smaller and rounder. What does this model?
c: weathering of rocks in a river
items.e: Shaking models rocks bumping in moving water.

items.q: Kai reads: “A glacier slides down a valley and shapes it.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes thousands of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Wind drops sand behind a fence and a small dune forms. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Pinnacles in Nambung National Park?
items.e: Wind blew away the sand around pillars of limestone.

items.q: Which process mainly formed London Arch near Port Campbell?
items.e: Waves wore away the cliff and made an arch; part of it fell in 1990.

items.q: A stream table has water flowing on a gentle slope. Where will most sand be dropped?
c: at the top, where the water starts
in the middle of the fastest part
at the bottom, where the water spreads out and slows
items.e: Slow water deposits sand.

items.q: Ethan reads: “A cave forms as water dissolves rock.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: thousands of years.

items.e: The steepest slope (35°) lost 155 g.

items.q: Jack says, 'Weathering and erosion are the same thing.' Which reply is best?
c: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves the pieces away.
Erosion breaks rock; weathering moves it.
items.e: One breaks, the other moves.

In Kai's test, what must stay the same for a fair test?
c: the amount of water and the type of soil
items.e: Only the slope should change.

items.q: Waves carve a cave into the bottom of a limestone cliff. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

c: The steeper the slope, the less soil was eroded.

items.q: Which variable should stay the same when testing how slope affects erosion?
c: the amount of soil washed away
items.e: Only the slope should change.

c: The channel became deeper because more sand was eroded.

items.q: Isla reads: “A big storm wave knocks down part of a sand dune.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: hours.

items.q: In a stream table, which change would carry the most sand away?
c: the same slope and no water
a flatter slope and less water
a steeper slope and more water
items.e: Faster water erodes and carries more.

items.q: A beach lost 3 m of sand in a big storm. Over the next 6 months it gained 1 m back each 2 months. How wide is it now compared with before the storm?
items.e: Erosion in the storm, deposition afterwards: 1 m × 3 = 3 m.

items.q: Chloe reads: “A rock falls off a cliff.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: seconds.

items.q: Kai blows through a straw at a pile of sand and gravel. What does he see?
c: The fine sand moves further than the gravel.
The gravel moves further than the sand.
items.e: Wind can carry light pieces further.

items.q: Mia reads: “A flood fills a town's streets with water.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: hours or days.

items.e: The steepest slope (25°) lost 140 g.

items.q: Ethan reads: “A tall mountain wears down and gets shorter.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a slow change: millions of years.

items.q: Ruby photographs a creek bank every month for a year. The bank moves back 40 cm. Which question does this answer?
c: How fast is the creek eroding its bank?
What will the weather be tomorrow?
How many fish live in the creek?
items.e: Repeated photos measure slow change.

items.q: Ella builds two model sand dunes. She covers one with spinifex grass cuttings and blows a fan at both. What is she testing?
items.e: The plants are the variable she changed.

items.q: Rain running off a car park cuts a channel in the dirt beside it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.
